stories.summary: Amit has Ajay say two words so he can feel the difference between dental sounds, where the tongue touches the upper teeth, and retroflex sounds, where the tongue curls back towards the roof of the mouth. Dental sounds run through Sanskrit's whole language family. Retroflex sounds do not, but they appear in all the Dravidian languages. Madhav Deshpande's 1976 essay, which Peggy Mohan cites, showed that even the Rig Veda's language had picked these sounds up from languages already spoken here. That stunned people who saw Sanskrit as pure. Peggy's explanation is that the migrants were mostly men who married local women, and the children spent their first years with mothers who spoke a different tongue. Amit adds that he was taught in school that all Indian languages come from Sanskrit, which is untrue. Tamil may well be older, and Tony Joseph suggests the Indus Valley language evolved into the Dravidian languages.
stories.insight: Even the 'purest' sacred language is a mixture. Language evolves through spontaneous order, and the mothers quietly reshaped the newcomers' tongue. One small fact about sounds undoes both the 'pure origin' story and the 'Sanskrit is the mother of all Indian languages' story.
stories.quote: But then you realize that what is really happening here is that it itself is a khichdi. You know, it is not one thing.

stories.topic: How Local Gods Joined the Family
stories.summary: As the Vedic Brahmins fanned out across the subcontinent, they lacked the political power to impose their beliefs. So they absorbed local beliefs and told stories about them, and these stories became the Puranas. In Andhra, instead of calling the Chenchu tribe savages, a myth had Vishnu consort with a Chenchu woman, and their child becomes the Chenchu god. In Tamil country, Ayyanar became Shiva's son by a beguiling female form of Vishnu. In 12th-century Maharashtra, Vitthal was declared a form of Vishnu even as some locals protested that he belonged to the Jain tradition. The rough rule was that Shaivites expanded Shiva's family, while Vaishnavites made the local god an avatar. Manu Pillai calls the Puranas 'works of genius' because they tied the local to the pan-Indian.
stories.insight: Hinduism's unity was built by accommodation rather than conquest. Rivals were absorbed into the family tree instead of being erased.
stories.quote: While for Vishnu, if you're up against a major local god, just make the dude an avatar and you're completely fine there.

stories.topic: The Lakshman Rekha Isn't in Valmiki
stories.summary: Drawing on AK Ramanujan's essay '300 Ramayanas', Amit shows how the epic kept being rewritten across regions and centuries. Surpanakha is ugly in Valmiki but beautiful in Kamban. In the Telugu version, Urmila sleeps for fourteen years: half for herself and half for Lakshman, so he can stay awake. The Lakshman Rekha, now a universal metaphor for a line one must not cross, first appears in Krittivasa's 15th-century Bengali version. Krittivasa also invents a particular washerman who starts the gossip about Sita. Versions disagree about who built the bridge to Lanka, and in some, Lav and Kush are one person rather than two.
stories.insight: The epics are 'open source', more like rivers than fixed texts. Some of today's most 'traditional' ideas are later regional additions, and this multiplicity is a feature, not a flaw.
stories.quote: I think it's a beautiful thing that, you know, a book being like a river, you never step into the same river twice, so you never step into the same Ramayana twice, and that's amazing.

stories.topic: Islam Came First as a Trader
stories.summary: The first Muslims in India were not invaders but peaceful traders on the Kerala coast; some say this happened within Muhammad's lifetime. Amit suggests this may be one reason communal feeling can seem lower in the south. The raiders came from the north, and they did destroy temples. But once rule settled, syncretism followed. In Sindh, Ali was adopted as an avatar of Vishnu, and in Maharashtra one god was also worshipped by some Muslims. In classic battles between a Mughal emperor and a Hindu rebel, half the emperor's generals were Hindu, and Amit recalls Turkish mercenaries fighting for Shivaji.
stories.insight: A clean Hindu-versus-Muslim binary flattens centuries of trade, intermarriage and shared worship, even as a sense of 'us versus an other' slowly began to form.
stories.quote: you'll find that half the generals of the Mughal Emperor were Hindu.

stories.topic: The Ox-God and the Kidnapping Syndicates
stories.summary: Missionaries were not always paid by the merchants and had to raise funds back home. Like a modern NGO, they played up the most extreme version of events. One Italian missionary invented a half-man, half-ox god who demanded the blood of 400 virgins. In this story, Indian parents gave up children to be beheaded, much as Christian parents gave children to the church. Others sent home erotic fantasies. In one, lonely widows at the shrine of Akbar's grandson took their pick of male pilgrims. In another, powerful women ran gangs that kidnapped men off the street for a night. These accounts shaped Europe's view of India. Voltaire read them and called it a barbarous nation, and James Mill wrote a history of India without ever visiting.
stories.insight: Who pays for knowledge shapes what that knowledge says. A fundraising incentive turned reports on India into tabloid fiction, and Europe's great thinkers built their picture of India on it.
stories.quote: If things are kinda good, you're not gonna say things are kinda good because you're not gonna get money.

stories.topic: Ten Thousand Satis That Were Thirty-Eight
stories.summary: One report claimed ten thousand satis in a single year; when Manu Pillai checked, the real figure was 38. The accounts also explained sati with a strange incentive story. Indian women were supposedly lecherous and unfaithful, so men feared their wives would kill them to be with other lovers, and ensured that widows would burn with them. Amit notes that this mirrors medieval Europe, where in some places unfaithful wives were burnt at the stake. The outsiders were projecting their own evils onto India.
stories.insight: Even a real social evil got distorted by exaggeration and projection. Reasoning about incentives, when built on wrong assumptions, produces confident nonsense.
stories.quote: Now 38 is still 38 too many, but you know, the numbers are out of whack.

stories.topic: The Missionary Who Was Told to Back Off
stories.summary: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg arrived with the usual missionary impulse to convert. But the more he engaged, the more he found, including much wisdom in the later Vedas. He wrote to his superiors that they had got it wrong: there was nothing to teach these people, because the best of their own learning was already mirrored in Indian teachings. His superiors slapped him down. Amit says Manu documents many such respectful dialogues and debates, but they were a small minority within a shrill discourse.
stories.insight: Real engagement tends to dissolve contempt, but institutions punish those who report it. Thoughtful conversation has always been a narrow band, then as now.
stories.quote: There is nothing we have to teach them. The best of our learnings are mirrored somewhere or the other in their teachings.

stories.summary: Ajay asks when missionaries became politically important, given that the Portuguese first came to Calicut for pepper. Amit says missionaries never dominated the merchants until the Industrial Revolution. Earlier missionaries were professionals in formal orders such as the Jesuits. Now anyone could become one; Manu writes about a shoemaker who came out. These freelancers competed for attention, and the journals printing their accounts sold in the hundreds of thousands. At the end of the 18th century, the British were still telling missionaries to hold back. Within twenty years that had flipped, and missionary zeal fed into governance, increasing both religious oppression and the reaction to it.
stories.insight: A change the hosts celebrate for spreading prosperity also had a hidden side effect. It lowered the barrier to entry for missionary work and turned it into a competitive media market.
stories.quote: But one of the side effects was that it created a category of people called the freelance missionary.

stories.topic: How 'Sanskari' Prudishness Came from the Victorians
stories.summary: Once the British began governing, they imposed their own laws and Victorian morality rather than adapting to local custom. In the original Shakuntala, the heroine is sweaty and sultry, and William Jones's translation drains away that sensuality. In The Ivory Throne, Manu Pillai wrote that it was once common for women in Kerala to be bare-breasted, until the British came and couldn't deal with it. The irony is that the same Europe sending home erotic fantasies about India was imposing prudery on it.
stories.insight: Much of what is defended today as traditional Indian modesty is a colonial import.
stories.quote: We think of, you know, behaving in certain ways as Sanskari. Actually the prudish behavior is not Indian at all. You know, it is something that the Victorians brought in.

stories.topic: Ram Mohan Roy: From Seeker to Columnist
stories.summary: Raja Ram Mohan Roy wrote his first book, Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin, in Persian, the language of the elites. It held radical views on religion and was a genuine quest to understand the world. Later, writing in Bengali, he became more like a modern columnist trying to persuade people. He was anglicised, comfortable with the British, and even went to London as the Mughal emperor's emissary. He drew on the Upanishads and later Vedas to argue that Hinduism resembled Western philosophy rather than being polytheistic. His aims were to modernise the faith and to win British respect. The Brahmo Samaj he founded was the version the British liked, since 'these people make for good babus'. Its line runs to Tagore, with Vivekananda in a similar vein.
stories.insight: A reformer arguing for an audience's approval ends up shaping the religion to fit that audience. The result is respectable, but elite.
stories.quote: he has really now become what a modern columnist would be, that he's trying to convince people of a point of view.

stories.topic: Dayanand Saraswati, the Mouse and the Corpse
stories.summary: One night at a Shiva temple, Dayanand Saraswati watched a mouse eat the prasad left for the idol. He expected the god to strike it dead, but nothing happened, and he began to question. He travelled and spent a few years with a hermit. Once, on the banks of the Ganga, he cut open a corpse to check whether the body matched its description in the scriptures; it didn't. He cared nothing for the British and was disgusted by the Puranic melange. He sought a purer faith rooted in the early Vedas and founded the Arya Samaj. At the Brahmo Samaj in Kolkata he learned that he had to speak the people's language, so he began writing in Hindi. He also learned pamphleteering, publicity, marketing and brand building from them.
stories.insight: A single falsifying observation can launch a movement. And the elite rival taught him the mass-marketing tools that would help his movement outlast theirs.
stories.quote: And he says, Oh my God, this is the idol of Shiva, the God will strike the mouse down dead, nothing happens, a mouse eats a prasad and goes away.

stories.topic: Tilak Takes Religion to the Streets
stories.summary: Amit finds Bal Gangadhar Tilak odious in many of his views; he opposed girls being educated, for instance. But Tilak was a deeply astute political strategist who saw that a movement couldn't be built in elite drawing rooms. He did two big things. First, he revived Shivaji as a brand, as one of the earliest articulators of Hindu-versus-the-other. Second, he took Ganapati, a local festival not then celebrated at scale, and made it a grand public celebration that brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets. That common identity could then be used for other purposes. What he never did was define what Hinduism is.
stories.insight: Political identity is built through ritual and mass mobilisation before it is built through theory. Backward views and strategic brilliance can live in the same person.
stories.quote: He realizes that if I want to build a political movement, we can't talk about it in elite drawing rooms. we have to go out there and, you know, rouse the masses.

stories.summary: Having read nearly all of Savarkar's biographies, Amit sees two Savarkars. Until 1910 he is a Bhagat Singh-like revolutionary who organises revolutionary acts. His book was praised by Nehru, he shared a London stage with Gandhi, and he insisted that Hindus and Muslims must throw off the yoke together. Then he was jailed in the Andamans as a terrorist rather than a political prisoner, far from the genteel imprisonment Nehru got. Between the British jailers and the prisoners stood a layer of mostly Pathan guards who brutalised the inmates, and there are rumours of worse than torture. He came out around 1920 radicalised and hating Muslims, and wrote Essentials of Hindutva. Amit first found the book lousy and incoherent, before seeing its political genius.
stories.insight: An ideology can carry the imprint of one man's trauma. Had Savarkar died in 1910, he would be remembered entirely differently.
stories.quote: There is a Savarkar till 1910, and there is a Savarkar that comes later.

stories.summary: The Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad told Amit on The Seen and the Unseen that his heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith. Amit finds this utterly resonant. He points to the growth after 1991 that lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, including hundreds of millions of Dalits.
stories.insight: Diagnosis and remedy can come from different traditions. Pairing the great critic of caste with the economist of markets dissolves a false choice.
stories.quote: Ambedkar lets you know how deep the problems are and how they cannot be solved within the current system, but Adam Smith gives you the way out.

recommendations.item: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
recommendations.creator: Manu Pillai
recommendations.context: Amit's primary source for the episode, which he recommends again in the closing segment.
recommendations.reason: Its introductory essay, 'A Brief History of Hinduism', synthesises the Puranic period so beautifully that he urges everyone to go out and buy the book. It is also the source of much of the colonial-era material: the missionaries, the sati figures and the reformers.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Manu Pillai
recommendations.context: Amit's recent episode with Manu Pillai on his new book; Amit says he discussed Savarkar there in detail.
recommendations.reason: The fuller version of this story, especially on Savarkar. 'You should listen to that.'

recommendations.item: Devdutt Pattanaik and the Stories That Shape Us (Episode 404 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Devdutt Pattanaik
recommendations.context: The twelve-hour episode with the mythologist that Amit recorded just before the one with Manu.
recommendations.reason: A deep immersion in Indian mythology. Devdutt's books are among the first things Amit recommends at the end.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Arshia Sattar
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier episode on the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.
recommendations.reason: Background for the episode's argument that the epics are open-source rivers rather than fixed texts.

recommendations.item: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
recommendations.creator: Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Mentioned at the start and again when discussing Hindutva's rise.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece that showed him aspects of society he didn't know. It traces what was happening in the culture over the decades, and shows how strong Hinduism's hold on the imagination was.

recommendations.item: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Amit's 'great episode' with Akshaya Mukul, cited while explaining Hindutva's cultural soil.
recommendations.reason: The conversational companion to the book, on how culture and religion fed into modern political Hinduism.

recommendations.creator: Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: Recommended for the deep-history section; Ajay also cites its account of the migration route.
recommendations.reason: Uses genetic evidence to tell how we got here, including the coastal route into India. It also suggests that the Indus Valley language evolved into the Dravidian languages.

recommendations.item: Tony Joseph's episode on The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
recommendations.context: Named at the start as relevant to the episode's opening history.
recommendations.reason: The audio version of the genetic history of the subcontinent.

recommendations.creator: Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Source of the retroflex-sounds discussion.
recommendations.reason: Shows that Sanskrit absorbed local sounds, and explains how male migrants marrying local women blended languages over generations.

recommendations.item: Understanding India Through Its Languages (Episode 232 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
recommendations.context: Named at the start as relevant to the episode.
recommendations.reason: Peggy Mohan's linguistic history of India in conversation.

recommendations.item: Who We Are and How We Got Here
recommendations.creator: David Reich
recommendations.context: Recommended twice in the deep-history section.
recommendations.reason: Explains how modern genetics reconstructs human history, including the science behind the Aryan migration that Amit doesn't have time to go into. Also the source of the point that the Germanic invasion of Rome would be invisible in the archaeology too.

recommendations.item: Father Returning Home
recommendations.creator: Dilip Chitre
recommendations.context: Amit reads it in full to open the story.
recommendations.reason: One of his favourite poems. Its closing image of 'nomads entering a subcontinent through a narrow pass' launches the episode's journey into deep history.

recommendations.item: Ahimsa: 100 Reflections on the Harappan Civilization
recommendations.creator: Devdutt Pattanaik
recommendations.context: Devdutt's new book on Harappa, cited in the Indus Valley section.
recommendations.reason: Offers a frame Amit loves: Harappan cities prioritised traders over raiders, and ahimsa is voluntary exchange between consenting adults.

recommendations.item: The History and Geography of Human Genes
recommendations.creator: Luca Cavalli-Sforza
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining how the Aryan migration debate was finally settled.
recommendations.reason: Showed that genetic evidence can reveal, with surprising certainty, when people arrived somewhere and who they mixed with.

recommendations.item: Genesis of Rgvedic Retroflexion
recommendations.creator: Madhav Deshpande
recommendations.context: Cited via Peggy Mohan in the language discussion.
recommendations.reason: A 1976 essay that 'pretty much blew everyone away' by showing that the Rig Veda's language was influenced by what was spoken here before.

recommendations.item: A Prehistory of Hinduism
recommendations.creator: Manu Devadevan
recommendations.context: Quoted, via Manu Pillai, in the Puranic section.
recommendations.reason: Argues that worshipping Shiva or Vishnu was simply part of everyday life and not a marker of identity.

recommendations.item: 300 Ramayanas
recommendations.creator: AK Ramanujan
recommendations.context: The basis of the 'open-source epics' chapter.
recommendations.reason: A 'great essay' showing the Ramayana constantly rewritten across times and places according to local customs.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Swapna Liddle

recommendations.reason: Their dear friend Devangshu Datta is a Brahmo Samaji and talks about it in the episode.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
recommendations.context: Cited during the discussion of Savarkar's Hindutva.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
recommendations.context: Cited in the chapter on caste.
recommendations.reason: The conversation in which the Dalit scholar named Ambedkar and Adam Smith as his heroes, a pairing central to Amit's hope for ending caste.

core_ideas.concept: The Name May Be New, but the River Was Always There
core_ideas.explanation: Amit rejects two simple narratives. The first is the nationalist one: a glorious Hindu past was interrupted by invaders and must now be revived as a Hindu rashtra. The second is the academic one, which he held until recently. It says Hinduism is a recent construction: the word was coined by a Britisher in the late 18th century, Brahmin interlocutors sold the British a Vedic version, and the British fed that version back to Indians. Both are top-down simplifications. Following Manu Pillai, the truth is a continuous, plural tradition that only later acquired a name and borders.
core_ideas.quote: the name may be new, but the river was always there.

core_ideas.concept: We Are Layered Migrants, and Genetics Settled the Aryan Debate
core_ideas.explanation: Homo sapiens fossils appear in Africa about 300,000 years ago. The successful dispersal out of Africa came about 70,000 years ago; earlier migrants left no genetic trace. Humans reached the subcontinent around 65,000 to 60,000 years ago, travelling along the coast from near Basra into Kutch (Ajay, citing Tony Joseph). About 7,000 years ago, pastoralists from Iran settled at Mehrgarh, mixed with the earlier Indians, and this mixing led to the Harappan civilisation. Around 2100 BCE, migrants from the steppes arrived; they were mostly men, and they mixed with the locals. The 'Aryan invasion' became toxic partly because the Nazis loved the story, and partly because of the feeling that 'we are the original people'. Archaeology couldn't settle the question, but genetics can date the arrivals. Reich adds a caveat: the Germanic invasion of Rome would leave no archaeological trace either.
core_ideas.quote: Now we don't know whether they invaded or not, but there certainly was an Aryan migration.

core_ideas.explanation: Devdutt Pattanaik argues that Harappan city design reveals a society that prioritised traders over raiders. On this reading, ahimsa is more than non-violence: its fullest expression is voluntary exchange between consenting adults, which is exactly how one would describe free trade. Amit closes the episode on the same note. The great lesson of the modern world is cooperation and mutual benefit, and that is compatible with Hinduism.
core_ideas.quote: Ahimsa is not just nonviolence, but what is the ultimate sort of expression of it is actually peaceful trade.

core_ideas.explanation: The first is consolation. Facing death, those who tell themselves sustaining stories may pass on their genes better, so we are wired for belief. The second is explanation. In a bewildering world, myth fills the gaps in our knowledge (the 'God of the gaps'), which is why the earliest gods were nature gods; science has steadily taken over those gaps. The third is codification. A society's natural ways of behaving get written into its religion, not just the other way round. Ajay adds an evolutionary layer: in bands of about 150 hunter-gatherers, religiosity produced coherence, and the more coherent bands won wars, so genes predisposing people to belief were favoured.
core_ideas.quote: We're all gonna die. Life is nasty, brutish and short. What do you do? You gotta tell yourself a story that makes you go on.

core_ideas.explanation: In the Puranic period, Hinduism was curated from the bottom up, through people's lives and rituals, rather than decreed from above. Beliefs shifted gradually across space; Ajay compares this to language changing every hundred kilometres. Kings found Brahmin narratives useful for legitimacy, and Brahmins edged towards influence without pushing hard enough to tear the fabric. Meanwhile, Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists feuded and satirised each other. Brahmins themselves varied hugely: some were vegetarian and some not, some cremated their dead and some buried them. The simplistic narratives are top-down; the reality was emergent.
core_ideas.quote: I almost think of religion in this period as a curation driven by spontaneous order. You know, this is a religion forming itself from the bottom up

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks whether Hinduism stayed malleable because it was vast, oral and pre-printing press. In religions with a single, error-corrected written book, the book becomes a boundary that blocks organic evolution. Amit agrees and extends the point. When the British census made everyone record their caste, it arguably froze caste in place.
core_ideas.quote: Because what happens when you write something down is that it becomes ossified.

core_ideas.explanation: Manu Devadevan argues that worshipping Shiva or Vishnu once conferred no identity. Wearing cotton never made anyone a 'cotton wearer', and living in a thatched hut never made anyone a 'hut dweller'. Amit's analogy is liking black clothes versus white: a preference, not a tribe. Religious labels hardened later, with colonial definitions.
core_ideas.quote: worshipping a deity was simply a part of everyday life, not a marker of identity.

core_ideas.explanation: This is Mancur Olson's frame. A roving bandit grabs everything and leaves, so he has no reason to preserve anything. A stationary bandit stays, wants a steady flow of revenue, governs, fits in, and eventually becomes 'of the people', as the Mughals did by marrying Rajput princesses. Applied to Islamic rule in India, destruction happened mainly at the expanding edges; once rule was settled came coexistence, court life and intermarriage (Richard Eaton has written about this). Ajay adds a caution: the medieval world was horrific everywhere and had no good guys, so singling out some cruelties and judging them by today's standards misleads.
core_ideas.quote: He doesn't want to kill the goose that will lay the golden eggs.

core_ideas.concept: A Common Enemy Forges a Common Identity
core_ideas.explanation: Before the invasions, the people later called Hindus were at loggerheads, with worshippers of Shiva and Vishnu fighting each other. A common enemy made them start seeing themselves as politically unified, though the word 'Hindu' came later. Colonialism sharpened this, as in Manu Pillai's image of four squabbling brown-skinned men who discover their shared brownness only when a white man attacks them all. The earlier Brahmins had assimilated others, but the colonisers wanted to rule, so assimilation was no longer an option and a counter-story had to be built.
core_ideas.quote: Suddenly white guy comes in and they feel the sense of unity and that sense of unity becomes a unified identity.

core_ideas.explanation: When something is too complex to grasp, the mind craves closure and invents a story, possibly a false one. Europeans facing an open-source religion they couldn't grok simplified it in several ways. They adopted a Brahminical, caste-based view, ran a census in which everyone ticked a box, and pushed these narratives through education. This reshaped how Indians saw themselves. As Sudipta Kaviraj puts it, giving itself a history is a community's most fundamental act of self-identification.
core_ideas.quote: you can't grok it. But you need closure, right? The complexity is too hard for you to deal with. So therefore you make up a story about it, which is possibly false

core_ideas.explanation: Savarkar's political masterstroke was to make Hindutva the umbrella term, with Hinduism as only one part of it. To belong, two conditions must both hold: India must be your homeland, and India must be your holy land. This excludes the British, and also Muslims, who turn to Mecca, while bringing in Buddhists, Jains, Shaivites, Vaishnavites and Dalits. Nobody asked why the line should be drawn there; it simply worked politically. Amit sees this as a radical departure: a tradition defined by absorbing the multitudes was now built on hard othering.
core_ideas.quote: Hinduism is a subset of Hindutva.

core_ideas.concept: Caste Will Erode from the Bottom Up, Through Markets
core_ideas.explanation: Amit calls caste a deep problem; he often calls it Hinduism's original sin, though he notes it isn't original as such. It is a social evil, like sati, and it has to go. Top-down fixes disappoint. Savarkar insisted Dalits belonged, and repeatedly held inter-caste feasts in Ratnagiri that angered Brahmins. Modern Hindutva claims to have united the Hindu vote, but in practice the BJP worked existing fault lines like every party does. In UP it courted non-Jatav Dalits against Mayawati's Jatav base; in Maharashtra, non-Maratha OBCs. Amit's hope lies in markets and growth, which change incentives: there is less casteism in cities, and those who discriminate pay a price in a free market. Change will be slow, because 'paradigms change one funeral at a time'.
core_ideas.quote: A rupee is a rupee, whether a Dalit is paying you or a Brahmin is paying you.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's observation is that the very poor are not especially oriented towards religion. Religiosity peaks in the middle, and secularisation arrives once societies become rich, educated and connected to the world. India's 1991 reforms created a middle class that began asserting its identity, which puts India at the religious peak of the middle stage. In time, secularisation will come for India too.
core_ideas.quote: In time secularization will come for India as well.

core_ideas.concept: Why the Genteel Elite Vision Lost
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that the humanist Hinduism of Ram Mohan Roy, Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru seemed settled to his parents' generation, but the last twenty years have shown another face of the country. Amit says that vision was bound to fail, because its champions were Westernised elites who were sometimes condescending to the masses. History had already signalled this. When Dayanand died, the elites expected the Brahmo Samaj to thrive and the Arya Samaj to fade, and the reverse happened. Real reform comes from below. Dayanand and Tilak took it in a direction Amit dislikes, but other directions are possible.
core_ideas.quote: They were deracinated elites, they were as influenced by the West as by India.

core_ideas.concept: Hinduism Is Compatible with a Liberal Life
core_ideas.explanation: Amit, a non-believer, argues that Hinduism holds values compatible with classical liberalism: respect for women, no divisions in society, consent. It is still a khichdi. Practising Hindus still visit dargahs and eat biryani on Eid; we may hate 'the other' in the abstract, but in the concrete we mingle. His own values, he says, are not foreign values; they are 'in the air around us'.
core_ideas.quote: to be a good Hindu is perhaps to just embrace all of the world as it is and look at it with love.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit addresses English-speaking urban elites who have never engaged with Hinduism. He asks them not to be condescending, because this is not infra-dig stuff. To understand yourself you must understand your society, and to understand your society you must understand the deep past. Read history to understand how things came to be, while keeping your own values intact.
core_ideas.quote: Remember all of the things that you're reading are description, not prescription. They are explanation and not exculpation.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After noting that the Lakshman Rekha first appears in Krittivasa's Bengali Ramayana, Amit says: 'See, Bengali is being normative again, we know best, we'll tell you what to do.'

One of the missionaries' invented tales was about women who ran gangs that kidnapped men off the street for a night. In it, a woman has a man kidnapped 'only to find out it is her own lawfully wedded husband.'

Judging by the stories missionaries sent home, Amit concludes that 'Europe at this point must have been deeply sexually repressed', and calls these tales 'a mad fantasy of some bored, frustrated missionary somewhere.'

Ziegenbalg's superiors respond to his praise of Indian wisdom with, in effect, 'fuck off, what are you doing?' Amit says they were accusing him of Stockholm syndrome, 'though of course the term didn't exist then.'

On how small the space for civil discourse was in colonial times: 'somewhere that age also has an Amit Varma and Ajay Shah and they're chatting with the British interlocutors and everything is civil. But that's a small part of it.'
On how invasion united feuding sects: 'a common enemy comes who says, Stop this show, you're all going to jail. Right? And instantly we unite against that common enemy.'
Amit raises his own line: 'I used to think there are as many Hinduisms as there are Hindus. I actually think there are more Hinduisms than there are Hindus.'

Amit opens with Dilip Chitre's poem 'Father Returning Home'. In it, a tired father gets off the train 'like a word dropped from a long sentence' and falls asleep 'thinking of nomads entering a subcontinent through a narrow pass.'
Game of Thrones: Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists destroying each other's places of worship is 'actually like Game of Thrones, that people are just going mad.'
Harry Potter: the Vedas are not 'one series like the Harry Potter series'. They were composed over ages, and the early and later Vedas are startlingly different.
The Basava Purana satirises Brahmins: it opens with a dog reciting the Vedas and mocks the idea of purifying oneself after seeing someone.
The Nazis took the term 'Aryan' from accounts of the Aryan invasion and the swastika from Hindu tradition. Amit gives this as one reason the migration became such a toxic topic.
MG Ranade said that in the Puranic period Hinduism 'was conquered by the multitudes', meaning it not only contains multitudes but was made by them.
Dilip Menon, on Puranic syncretism: 'deceased ancestors, local heroes and heroines, gods of the Vedic pantheon and nature gods all rubbed shoulders in a seamless fabric of worship.'
Purushottam Agrawal on colonial law: 'instead of cutting the cloth to fit the body, they cut the body to fit the cloth.'
Shruti Kapila: Hindutva is 'a theory of violence in search of a history'. Savarkar supplied the history.
Richard Eaton 'has written wonderfully well' about how, once the Mughal empire settled, violence was confined to its expanding edges.

Amit's heroes among the Congress moderates are Ranade, Gokhale and Agarkar, 'men who follow liberal ends through conservative means' and who didn't want to burn everything down. They were set against extremists like Tilak.

Jyotirao Phule, with his formidable wife, questioned both caste and the confinement of women at a time when other 'reformers' didn't. Amit calls their work 'a great movement worth studying in great depth'.
On syncretic food, Amit nods to an earlier Everything is Everything episode on 'how all the food that you think is Indian actually came from somewhere else.'
